assumptions.summary: Temperature and humidity remain in a narrow event-time range. Boundary: This narrows environmental variation but lacks venue observations and does not remove air-density uncertainty.
Equal output for equal time consumes equal normalized resource across physical states. Boundary: This enables additive depletion but excludes recovery and history dependence.
Mechanical loss is fixed at five percent. Boundary: This supports eta=0.95 only if drivetrain conditions are calibrated and remains separate from physiological reserve.
Total turn length is small enough that turn time and transitions can be neglected. Boundary: Length share alone does not bound braking, acceleration, energy, or safety effects.
Output is constant on each classified section. Boundary: This creates a tractable and communicable strategy but needs grid convergence and execution-rate limits.
Selected small angles have sufficiently linear response for length-weighted aggregation. Boundary: The approximation needs an objective and decision error bound.

Literature position drag effects and staged formation switches transfer to the modeled team. Boundary: Individual fatigue, rotation, geometry, switching cost, and fourth-finisher state are not closed.

contributions.summary: Makes response-model selection conditional on three physiological regimes and previews the complete interface chain.
Turns an inverse response curve into a shared normalized resource constraint with an explicit operational reserve.
Separates physical loads before constructing a speed interface for optimization.
Combines a transparent turn bound with a terrain-conditioned section optimizer.
Uses small-angle structure to reduce the Belgium optimizer and makes the aggregation rule visible.
Uses a default/exception architecture for Tokyo regular and special roads.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Four rider-profile rows at five durations provide the sparse response inputs. Learning: Preserve measured values separately from derived physiology and require row-level provenance, sample definition, and uncertainty.
CP, reserve, maximum output, and transition values are derived from Table 2. Learning: Keep derived status, equation provenance, units, and the reserve/threshold ambiguities explicit.

A Webots course provides a synthetic geometry with turns and grade. Learning: Treat the image as a testbed description; raw coordinates, lengths, slopes, generation seed, and export procedure are absent.

Official route information and Google Earth are used to derive Belgium's 32 sections. Learning: Record source-to-segment provenance but require measurement resolution, error, coordinates, and raw class arrays.
Tokyo is divided into 68 segments and 62 regular sections. Learning: Retain counts and exception identities while marking full length/slope/membership arrays as unavailable.
Local geometry and values support sections 24-27 as an exception complex. Learning: Use only after units, source, and cross-section parameter transfer are verified.
Local values are intended to support sections 55-56. Learning: The malformed table is retained as diagnostic provenance and excluded from trusted parameter ingestion.
Position-dependent drag ratios are imported from cited team-formation evidence. Learning: Require the coefficient table, geometry, conditions, and rider matching before numerical use.

edges.handoff: T(Pout), with output in W/kg and holding time in the source's mixed time scale, becomes the denominator of normalized depletion.
The dimensionless accumulated-use terminal constraint is fixed at 0.95 for the synthetic-course optimizer.
Road-conditioned speed functions in m/s convert section lengths and output decisions into travel time.
Turn-specific maximum speed and converted output are compared with the piecewise straight/ramp strategy.
The common time objective, resource constraint, and terrain-condition speed functions are reused on Belgium after route segmentation.
The common optimizer is reused for Tokyo regular sections after class grouping and exception removal.
The local turn-speed condition is combined with special-section geometry and reference straight decisions.
Special-section elapsed times in seconds are added to the regular-section total; a full energy/state reconciliation is not printed.
The aerodynamic resistance and output-speed interface are reevaluated under wind magnitude and angle perturbations.
The Belgium section target and 53.03-minute baseline seed the spline and execution-disturbance experiment.
The qualitative finding that frontal/headwind effects are larger than crosswind effects motivates formation selection; no numeric coefficient is directly transferred.

models.summary: MU-A-2022-2207343-M01: The paper combines a critical-power baseline, an exponential short-duration branch, and a full-power long-duration branch. Equations (1)-(3) estimate CP, reserve, and a transition; Table 4 supplies all three displayed branches. The output T(P) is consumed by the energy model. Handoff: T P CP Wprime

MU-A-2022-2207343-M02: A discrete sum of interval-specific fractions is replaced by an integral of 1/T(Pout). The ideal full-depletion equality is later implemented as 0.95 to reserve an operational buffer. Handoff: lambdaE T Pout

MU-A-2022-2207343-M03: The model sums rolling, slope, inertial, and aerodynamic loads, divides by stated drivetrain efficiency, and closes with m Pout = Ftotal v. This produces condition-specific speed functions consumed by the piecewise time objectives. Handoff: v Pout Ftotal

MU-A-2022-2207343-M04: A labeled cut-corner geometry and a tire-friction inequality are combined into the unnumbered equation (*). The result is used as a local limit and compared with straight-section strategies. Handoff: vmax R

MU-A-2022-2207343-M05: The course is split into seven straight, one downhill, and one uphill section, with turns treated by M04. Equation (12) minimizes summed section times subject to the 0.95 accumulated-resource constraint. Handoff: Pi Pj Pk Pout t

MU-A-2022-2207343-M06: Equation (13) instantiates the common objective. Equations (14)-(15) form a length-weighted composite of slopes below one degree, and Equation (16) replaces the selected set by one aggregate segment. Handoff: Pi Pk PC t

MU-A-2022-2207343-M07: Equation (17) groups selected two- and four-degree uphill/downhill classes in 62 regular sections. Sections 24-27 and 55-56 are excluded for M08 and then added back. Handoff: Pout Sigma_i Sigma_j Sigma_k Sigma_T t

MU-A-2022-2207343-M08: The paper uses local grade, geometry, speed, output, and a stated 20 m deceleration instruction for sections 24-27 and 55-56. It reports local times but no complete state equation or joint optimization. Handoff: v_local P_local t_local

MU-A-2022-2207343-M09: The paper perturbs a straight-road wind baseline and separately perturbs turn wind speed and local angle, then plots response error. No new governing equation is printed beyond reuse of M03/M04. Handoff: wind_speed gamma response_error

MU-A-2022-2207343-M10: A spline interpolation of the ideal step control is perturbed by four sine terms. Three executions are checked for terminal resource and time lag, and the paper recommends returning to the target at section ends. Handoff: Preal lambda_terminal time_result

MU-A-2022-2207343-M11: The paper compares long-snake, pyramid, shield, and diagonal formations, divides a 20 km course into Balance, Storage, and Sprint phases, and reports 48/27/25 shares. It prints no complete objective, coefficient table, rotation dynamics, or search equation. Handoff: formation LB LS LR team_time

results_trace.summary: Synthetic-course times are 47.53/48.58 minutes for male/female sprinters and 46.48/48.20 for male/female specialists. Boundary: Bind these values to the synthetic geometry, four category profiles, piecewise controls, and missing uncertainty.
The male specialist row reports 6.5, 6.4, and 5.1 W/kg for straight, uphill, and downhill classes. Boundary: Use as a scenario-specific terrain allocation, not a universal profile rule.
Turns A-E report outputs 2.94, 7.27, 4.94, 3.23, 12.13 and speeds 7.34, 11.02, 9.48, 7.98, 13.38. Boundary: Retain the values with the source's missing-unit and duration-feasibility boundary.
Belgium times are 58.15/59.62 minutes for sprinters and 53.03/54.05 for specialists. Boundary: Bind to the aggregated Belgium route and separate the 53.03 baseline used by execution testing.
Only sections 23 and 32 are identified as needing slight deceleration under the turn overlay. Boundary: This is a local constraint result contingent on the turn geometry and coefficient assumptions.

The reported local choices include 6.0 m/s and 6.32 W/kg for section 25, 6.4 m/s and 5.31 W/kg for section 27, totaling 31.2 s. Boundary: Retain as a local calculation with transferred-reference and acceleration boundaries.

Section 56 reports 5.806 m/s and 4.32 W/kg; the section 55 sequence reports 5.6 W/kg, 10.0 m/s, a 20 m slowdown, and 21.7 s total. Boundary: Use only as printed scenario output; Table 9 fields and transition dynamics are unresolved.
Tokyo times print 62.68, 56.03, 40.97, and 33.63 minutes in the table's four profile order. Boundary: Keep this table independent from the conflicting Table 11 values.

A nominally one-percent straight input perturbation produces a visually much larger output-error span. Boundary: Treat the plot as evidence of strong local sensitivity and a figure/prose inconsistency, not a ten-percent calibrated law.

The ideal and three perturbed terminal indicators are approximately 0.950, 0.975, 0.939, and 0.952. Boundary: All printed runs appear finish-feasible under the paper's criterion, but the test is not a population robustness estimate.
The ideal and three perturbed times are 53.03, 53.29, 54.38, and 53.59 minutes. Boundary: The worst lag is approximately 2.55%, not strictly within the printed 2.5% or Summary 2% boundary.
The model/champion pairs are printed as 56.03/55.08 and 34.63/30.22 minutes. Boundary: Retain for contradiction analysis only because profile values and implied errors do not reconcile.

The staged team result is 21.2 minutes against a 24.8-minute individual baseline over the reported 20 km model. Boundary: Treat as an unreproduced scenario result until the team objective and coefficients are printed.
The reported modeled average is 56.6 km/h versus a cited 56.1 km/h comparator. Boundary: This is contextual proximity, not matched validation.
Balance, Storage, and Sprint receive 48%, 27%, and 25% with pyramid, long-snake, and shield formations. Boundary: The shares and switches are recommendations without a printed derivation.

The artifact provides profile-dependent grade classes, percentage adjustments, curves, and a turn calculator. Boundary: Preserve the conditional translation pattern while withholding hard thresholds from deployment until calibration and safety checks exist.

section_map.summary: Seven visual paragraphs route Tasks 1-5, principal times, perturbation findings, team stages, and guidance.
Defines the response concept, decision value, full requirement ledger, fourth-finisher rule, and audience.
Bounds the two-parameter baseline and maps three physiological regimes to candidate methods.
Previews response, dynamics, course tests, sensitivity, and team extension with Figure 2.
States environmental, additive-resource, and fixed-loss assumptions with reasons.
Routes rider observations to derived parameters and response curves.
Converts holding time to a continuous normalized resource constraint.
Builds the force ledger and Pout-v interface.
Derives turn bounds and a piecewise nonlinear time optimizer on a controlled testbed.
Segments the official route, aggregates small slopes, solves controls, and checks turns.
Groups regular sections, isolates two special complexes, and combines results.
Scopes weather factors, evaluates wind, and tests execution deviations.
Uses position drag concepts to propose staged and crosswind formations.
Labels strengths/limits, proposes transfer, and recaps the model-to-decision chain.
Translates profile, grade, wind, and turn outputs into a two-page professional artifact.

All numbered Equations (1)-(17), Table 4's three branches, the unnumbered Pout-v closure, equation (*), and the two displayed execution expressions were visually reconciled.
Formula, table, and figure inconsistencies are retained as last-pass warnings rather than silently corrected.

unresolved_questions: Equation (2) prints 0.24 s times the three/twelve-minute difference, while Table 3 reserve values and its J/kg label imply a factor or unit-scale conflict; retain the source expression but forbid direct reuse until dimensionally reconciled.
Equation (3) uses an undefined P and Table 3 does not provide units for MAP_TTF or CP_TTF, so branch-boundary calculations are not operationally typed.
The source sets k=0.7 and A=0.1 by an asserted continuity requirement without printing their units, continuity equations, fit residuals, or uncertainty.
The aligned curves support an internal plausibility comparison only; sample size, matched profiles, source uncertainty, and external outcome validation are absent.
Summing fractions of maximal holding time assumes linear additive depletion across changing output and omits recovery below CP and path-dependent physiological state.

Mechanical transmission loss, drivetrain efficiency eta=0.95, and the terminal five-percent physiological reserve are three different interfaces and must not be merged, double-counted, or used to justify one another.
vwind is defined as wind speed but set equal to bicycle speed in no wind, so it functions as relative incident air speed in one place and ambient wind in another; direction and sign are missing.
The stated air density cannot be derived from temperature and humidity alone without pressure, and the venue/time distribution used for the value is not shown.
Cr is given only as a wide range, with no selected value or calibration for the plotted output-speed curves, preventing reproduction of rolling resistance.
The prose calls r an inner diameter while the geometry treats it like a radius; later tables also mix radius and angle fields, so the turn input convention is inconsistent.
The force sum, efficiency division, rider-mass-normalized output, and total rider-plus-bicycle mass do not receive one explicit dimensional and sign-convention closure.

The source uses total turn length relative to course length to ignore turn time and speed transitions, but short sharp turns can have nonproportional braking, acceleration, energy, and safety effects.
The strategy treats controls as section-boundary steps while Equation (10) retains acceleration and later guidance assumes finite braking; the state transition is not reconciled.
Equation (12) leaves the relationship between t and tn, control bounds, initial/final speeds, continuity, and the integration of local turn limits unspecified.
Mathematica Minimize is named without domains, starting values, precision, stopping rules, convergence status, grid size, or a discretization-refinement check.
Turn output and speed values lack units, and the reported 12.13 output for turn E cannot be checked against a duration-specific response constraint from the table alone.
Calling roughly 400 m long enough to hold an optimum is not supported by approach speed, acceleration time, braking distance, or a steady-state distance calculation.

Small-slope aggregation is motivated by approximate trigonometric linearity but no error is propagated to speed, chosen output, resource use, or completion time; Equation (14) is also visually ambiguous.

Rows labeled like #55km/#56km and values such as 0.2m, approximately 0m, 0 degrees, and 12 degrees appear under mismatched length/radius/angle fields, so Table 9 cannot be parsed as trusted parameters.
A 4.4-degree reference from section 63 is transferred to sections 24-27 without a transfer argument, while the 20 m braking and immediate recovery instructions omit acceleration constraints.
Temperature/humidity evidence from adjacent sport contexts and the claim that training mitigates rain do not close rain-related grip, braking, or safety effects for this event.
The weather sweep fixes grade at zero percent, so it cannot establish route-wide robustness on the multi-slope Belgium and Tokyo courses.
The source alternates among one-percent, ten-percent, one-to-four m/s, and plus/minus two m/s perturbations; Figure 18 appears to span roughly -27% to +34% while prose says an undefined ten percent.
The prose reports turn wind-direction and wind-speed effects near 0.1% and 0.01%, but Figure 20 reaches roughly +1.7% and -2.2%; the quantities cannot be treated as one result.
The four sine terms have no empirical frequency basis, phase, amplitude distribution, random seed, or spline boundary conditions, and three runs cannot establish general robustness.
The worst printed run is 54.38 against 53.03 minutes, about 2.55%, slightly above 'within 2.5%' and inconsistent with the Summary's 'within 2%'.
Table 10 prints specialist times 40.97/33.63, whereas Table 11 uses 56.03/34.63; 56.03 belongs to another profile in Table 10 and 34.63 differs from 33.63.
Table 11 model/champion pairs imply about 1.7% and 14.6% differences, not a shared approximately six-percent error; the claimed accuracy is not arithmetically reproducible.
A scenario calculation using average-profile inputs that lies near one champion time cannot show that the strategy causes an average athlete to achieve champion performance.
The team discussion announces a one-kilometer straight but the next page defines and reports a twenty-kilometer model, leaving the evaluation scenario inconsistent.
The 48/27/25 shares and 21.2-minute result have no printed objective, coefficient table, switch-cost model, search method, fourth-finisher state logic, or sensitivity.
A modeled 56.6 km/h value near the cited 56.1 km/h BMC speed does not prove accuracy because course, weather, riders, formation, and timing conditions are not matched.

The Anna van der Breggen/Tokyo champion/mathematician/Cambridge PhD chain requires external verification, while RIDERMAN, RIDEMAN, and RIDERMEN vary across the artifact; neither enters reusable factual evidence.
The 85/90-percent route thresholds, grade classes, hard output changes, and turning advice lack individual uncertainty and safety bounds; red/green dependence and tiny curves reduce accessibility.

No appendix or code publishes rider rows, route arrays, Webots geometry, Mathematica notebook, Python scripts, seeds, spline rule, formation coefficients, or plotted arrays, preventing end-to-end reproduction.

verification.summary: Aligned response curves show expected subgroup and duration ordering. Interpretation: This is an internal qualitative plausibility check; it cannot establish fit, uncertainty, or external predictive validity.

Rolling, aerodynamic, and total output-speed curves have the expected qualitative ordering. Interpretation: This checks mechanism direction only; missing coefficients and operating conditions prevent quantitative validation.

Straight/ramp decisions are compared with local turn limits to flag two binding turns. Interpretation: This is a constraint-consistency check, not a validation of braking dynamics or full-course time.

The controlled course is used to derive a method that is then instantiated on two official routes. Interpretation: This checks workflow portability but not transfer accuracy because route mechanisms and approximation errors are not matched.

Local perturbation curves compare the response to wind magnitude and direction in straight and turning regimes. Interpretation: This is local sensitivity; inconsistent ranges and figure/prose magnitudes prevent a general robustness claim.

Three execution perturbations are checked first for finish-resource feasibility and then for completion-time lag. Interpretation: This is a small demonstration with no distribution, seed, or interval; it cannot prove stable performance.

Model times are placed beside actual winners as an external comparator. Interpretation: The comparison is unmatched and internally inconsistent with Table 10, so it cannot support the printed common accuracy claim.
The modeled team speed is compared with a cited BMC value. Interpretation: The single contextual match lacks course, weather, roster, and timing alignment and is not external validation.

The authors label efficiency, accuracy, universality, and stability and point to models or scenario checks. Interpretation: Each label must be reduced to the exact artifact and scenario it cites; self-labeling adds no independent evidence.

The two-page artifact tests whether model outputs can be routed to a professional reader through profile and condition branches. Interpretation: This supports stakeholder translation structure only; operational thresholds, units, safety, and accessibility remain unvalidated.
